rubric.text: Term rewritten as $\tfrac1n\cdot\tfrac{(k/n)^2}{1+k/n}$, a Riemann sum for $f(x)=\tfrac{x^2}{1+x}$ on $[0,1]$

solution:
Factor $n^3$: $\dfrac{k^2}{n^2(n+k)}=\dfrac1n\cdot\dfrac{(k/n)^2}{1+k/n}$ (seq-limits, Riemann sum).
The limit is $\int_0^1\dfrac{x^2}{1+x}dx$ (ftc).
Divide: $\dfrac{x^2}{1+x}=x-1+\dfrac1{1+x}$ (poly-div).
$\Big[\tfrac{x^2}2-x+\ln(1+x)\Big]_0^1=\tfrac12-1+\ln2=\ln2-\tfrac12$.
hints: Pull out $\tfrac1n$ and write everything in terms of $k/n$.

prompt: Let $a_1=1$ and $a_{n+1}=\dfrac{a_n^2+6}{5}$ for $n\ge1$. Find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n$.

why: took the larger fixed point; the sequence stays below $2$
read the starting value as the limit

rubric.text: Monotone and bounded argued: if $0<a_n<2$ then $a_n<a_{n+1}<2$
Roots $2$ and $3$; limit is $2$ because the sequence starts at $1<2$ and never exceeds $2$

solution:
If $a_n<2$: $a_n^2-5a_n+6=(a_n-2)(a_n-3)>0$, so $a_{n+1}>a_n$; also $a_{n+1}<\tfrac{4+6}{5}=2$ (factor, induction on the bound).
So $(a_n)$ is increasing and bounded above by $2$, hence converges (seq-limits).
The limit satisfies $5L=L^2+6$, so $L^2-5L+6=0$ (quad): $L=2$ or $3$.
Only $L=2$ is reachable from $a_1=1$.
hints: Show monotone and bounded first, then take the limit in the recursion.

prompt: For which real $p$ does $\displaystyle\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n(\ln n)^p}$ converge?

why: assumed any decaying power of the log suffices
reversed the direction of the inequality
demanded a larger exponent than the integral test needs; the threshold is $p>1$

rubric.text: Terms positive and decreasing, so the integral test applies to $f(x)=\tfrac1{x(\ln x)^p}$
Substitution $u=\ln x$ turns the integral into $\int_{\ln2}^\infty u^{-p}\,du$
Convergence iff $p>1$; the case $p=1$ checked separately and diverges

solution:
For $n\ge2$ the terms are positive and decreasing, so use the integral test (series-tests).
$\int_2^\infty\dfrac{dx}{x(\ln x)^p}$ with $u=\ln x$, $du=\tfrac{dx}{x}$ (u-sub) becomes $\int_{\ln2}^\infty u^{-p}\,du$.
This converges iff $p>1$ (improper-int, $p$-test); at $p=1$ it is $\ln u\to\infty$.
hints: Compare with an integral and substitute $u=\ln x$.

prompt: For which $c>0$ does $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{c^n\,n!}{n^n}$ converge?

why: included $c=e$, where the terms are about $\sqrt{2\pi n}$ and do not tend to $0$
replaced the limit by its value $\tfrac12$ at $n=1$

rubric.text: Limit $\big(1+\tfrac1n\big)^{-n}\to e^{-1}$ found (e.g. by logarithms), so the ratio tends to $c/e$
Endpoint $c=e$ examined: terms do not tend to $0$, so diverges; answer $0<c<e$

solution:
Ratio test (series-tests): $\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\dfrac{c^{n+1}(n+1)!}{(n+1)^{n+1}}\cdot\dfrac{n^n}{c^nn!}=c\Big(\dfrac{n}{n+1}\Big)^n$.
$\ln\big(1+\tfrac1n\big)^{-n}=-n\ln(1+\tfrac1n)\to-1$ (log-diff, seq-limits), so the ratio tends to $c/e$.
Converges for $c<e$, diverges for $c>e$.
At $c=e$ the ratio stays above $1$ (since $(1+\tfrac1n)^n<e$), so the terms increase and the series diverges.
hints: Compute the ratio and handle $(1+1/n)^{-n}$ with a logarithm.

prompt: The alternating series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$ is approximated by its partial sum $S_N$. What is the smallest $N$ for which the alternating series bound guarantees $|S-S_N|<0.01$?

why: bounded the error by $a_N$ instead of $a_{N+1}$

rubric.text: Alternating series test conditions noted: terms decrease to $0$

solution:
Terms $\tfrac1{n^2}$ decrease to $0$, so the alternating series bound applies (alt-series).
$|S-S_N|\le a_{N+1}=\dfrac1{(N+1)^2}$.
Need $\dfrac1{(N+1)^2}<\dfrac1{100}$, i.e. $N+1>10$ (series-tests, seq-limits).
Smallest integer: $N=10$, since $N=9$ gives exactly $0.01$.
hints: The error is at most the first omitted term.
check: min([n for n in range(1,1000) if Fraction(1,(n+1)**2)<Fraction(1,100)])

prompt: Consider (I) $\sum\frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt n}$, (II) $\sum(-1)^n\sin\frac1n$, (III) $\sum(-1)^n\frac{n}{n+1}$, (IV) $\sum\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}$, all over $n\ge1$. How many are conditionally convergent?

why: thought alternating series never converge conditionally
judged (II) absolutely convergent because $\sin\tfrac1n$ is small

rubric.text: (I) converges by the alternating test, while $\sum n^{-1/2}$ diverges: conditional
(II) terms $\sin\tfrac1n$ positive, decreasing to $0$; $\sin\tfrac1n\sim\tfrac1n$ so the absolute series diverges: conditional
(III) terms tend to $\pm1$, diverges; (IV) absolutely convergent; total $2$

solution:
(I) $n^{-1/2}\downarrow0$, so converges (alt-series); $\sum n^{-1/2}$ diverges, so conditional.
(II) $\sin\tfrac1n\downarrow0$ so converges; $\lim\frac{\sin(1/n)}{1/n}=1$ (limit-special), so $\sum\sin\tfrac1n$ diverges by comparison with $\sum\tfrac1n$ (series-tests): conditional.
(III) $\tfrac{n}{n+1}\to1\neq0$, so the terms do not tend to $0$: diverges.
(IV) $\sum n^{-2}$ converges: absolute. Total: $2$.
hints: Check absolute convergence separately from the alternating test.

prompt: Find the interval of convergence of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(x-2)^n}{n\,3^n}$.

why: excluded both endpoints without testing them
included $x=5$, where the series is harmonic

solution:
Ratio: $\Big|\dfrac{(x-2)^{n+1}}{(n+1)3^{n+1}}\cdot\dfrac{n3^n}{(x-2)^n}\Big|\to\dfrac{|x-2|}{3}$, so $R=3$ about $2$ (power-series).
$x=5$: $\sum\tfrac1n$ diverges (series-tests).
$x=-1$: $\sum\tfrac{(-1)^n}{n}$ converges by the alternating test (alt-series).
Interval: $[-1,5)$.
hints: Test each endpoint separately.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^2}{2^n}$.

rubric.text: Geometric series $\sum x^n=\tfrac{x}{1-x}$ used as the starting point
Operator $x\tfrac{d}{dx}$ applied twice (derivative of a power series termwise) to get $\sum n^2x^n=\tfrac{x(1+x)}{(1-x)^3}$

solution:
Start with $\sum_{n\ge1}x^n=\dfrac{x}{1-x}$ for $|x|<1$ (seq-series, power-series).
Apply $x\frac{d}{dx}$ (deriv-rules): $\sum nx^n=\dfrac{x}{(1-x)^2}$.
Apply again: $\sum n^2x^n=x\cdot\dfrac{(1-x)+2x}{(1-x)^3}=\dfrac{x(1+x)}{(1-x)^3}$.
At $x=\tfrac12$: $\dfrac{\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac32}{\tfrac18}=6$.
hints: Differentiate the geometric series, then multiply by $x$.

rubric.text: Numerator reduces to $\big(\tfrac12-\tfrac1{24}\big)x^4+O(x^6)$, the $x^2$ terms cancelling with $\tfrac32x^2$

solution:
$e^{x^2}=1+x^2+\tfrac{x^4}{2}+O(x^6)$ and $\cos x=1-\tfrac{x^2}{2}+\tfrac{x^4}{24}+O(x^6)$ (taylor).
Difference: $\tfrac32x^2+\big(\tfrac12-\tfrac1{24}\big)x^4+O(x^6)$.
Subtract $\tfrac32x^2$ and divide by $x^4$ (limit-special): limit $\tfrac{11}{24}$.
L-Hopital would need four rounds of differentiation (lhopital); series is faster.
hints: Expand both functions to order $x^4$.

rubric.text: $e^{-x^2}=1-x^2+\tfrac{x^4}{2}-\tfrac{x^6}{6}+\cdots$ by substituting $-x^2$ into the exponential series

solution:
$e^{u}=\sum u^k/k!$ with $u=-x^2$ gives $e^{-x^2}=1-x^2+\tfrac{x^4}{2}-\cdots$ (taylor, exp-rules).
So $f(x)=x^2-x^4+\tfrac{x^6}{2}-\cdots$ (power-series).
The coefficient of $x^6$ is $\tfrac{f^{(6)}(0)}{6!}=\tfrac12$.
$f^{(6)}(0)=720\cdot\tfrac12=360$.
hints: Read the derivative off the coefficient of $x^6$.

prompt: Find the area of the region inside both of the polar curves $r=1$ and $r=2\cos\theta$.

why: gave the area of one full circle
sign error on $\sin2\theta$ at the lower limit

rubric.text: Area $=\tfrac\pi3+4\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$ set up using $\tfrac12\int r^2$ and symmetry
Half-angle evaluation gives $\tfrac\pi3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ for the second part; total $\tfrac{2\pi}3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$

solution:
Intersection: $2\cos\theta=1$ gives $\theta=\pm\tfrac\pi3$ (trig-eq). For $|\theta|<\tfrac\pi3$ the circle $r=1$ is closer to the origin; beyond that $r=2\cos\theta$ is (param-polar).
By symmetry, $A=2\Big[\tfrac12\!\int_0^{\pi/3}1\,d\theta+\tfrac12\!\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}4\cos^2\theta\,d\theta\Big]=\tfrac\pi3+2\!\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}(1+\cos2\theta)\,d\theta$ (trig-int).
$\big[2\theta+\sin2\theta\big]_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}=\pi-\big(\tfrac{2\pi}3+\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\big)=\tfrac\pi3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$.
$A=\tfrac\pi3+\tfrac\pi3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2=\tfrac{2\pi}3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$.
hints: Sketch both circles; the boundary switches curves at the intersection angle.

prompt: Find the length of the curve $x=t^2$, $y=t^3$ for $0\le t\le2$.

why: dropped the factor $\tfrac23$ when integrating $\sqrt u$

solution:
$x^{\prime}=2t$, $y^{\prime}=3t^2$, speed $=\sqrt{4t^2+9t^4}=t\sqrt{4+9t^2}$ (param-polar, arc-avg).
Let $u=4+9t^2$, $du=18t\,dt$, limits $4\to40$ (u-sub): $L=\tfrac1{18}\int_4^{40}\sqrt u\,du$.
$=\tfrac1{18}\cdot\tfrac23\big[u^{3/2}\big]_4^{40}=\tfrac1{27}\big(40^{3/2}-8\big)$.
$40^{3/2}=40\cdot2\sqrt{10}=80\sqrt{10}$, so $L=\tfrac{80\sqrt{10}-8}{27}$.
hints: Factor $t$ out of the speed so it can serve as $du$.

prompt: For $\mathbf u=\langle u_1,u_2,u_3\rangle$ and $\mathbf v=\langle v_1,v_2,v_3\rangle$, which vector is $\mathbf u\times\mathbf v$?

why: componentwise product, not the cross product
sign error in the middle component
dot product is a scalar, not a vector

solution: The $x$-component is $u_2v_3-u_3v_2$. The middle component is $u_3v_1-u_1v_3$, the opposite of the usual dot-pattern guess.
hints: Use the $2\times2$ minors with signs $+,-,+$ along the top row.

prompt: Which statement is true for nonzero vectors $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$?

options: $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=0$ exactly when $\mathbf u\perp\mathbf v$
$\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$ exactly when $\mathbf u\perp\mathbf v$
$\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=0$ exactly when $\mathbf u\parallel\mathbf v$
why: the cross product vanishes for parallel vectors
the dot product vanishes for perpendicular vectors
the cross product is a vector

solution: The dot product vanishes exactly when the vectors are perpendicular. The cross product vanishes exactly when they are parallel.
hints: Match each product to the geometric condition it detects.

prompt: Write $\lVert\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\rVert$ as an expression in $a=\lVert\mathbf u\rVert$, $b=\lVert\mathbf v\rVert$, and the angle $t$ between them.
solution: $\lVert\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\rVert=\lVert\mathbf u\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf v\rVert\sin t$. The magnitude is the area of the parallelogram.
hints: The cross product measures a parallelogram area.

prompt: Let $\mathbf u=\langle 1,-2,3\rangle$ and $\mathbf v=\langle 4,0,-1\rangle$. Find $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v$.
solution: $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=4+0-3=1$.
hints: Multiply matching components and add.

prompt: Let $\mathbf u=\langle 1,2,0\rangle$ and $\mathbf v=\langle 0,1,3\rangle$. Find the $x$-component of $\mathbf u\times\mathbf v$.
solution: The $x$-component is $u_2v_3-u_3v_2=2\cdot3-0\cdot1=6$.

prompt: Find $\|\langle 2,3,6\rangle\|$.
hints: Square each component, add, then take the root.

prompt: Find the scalar projection of $\mathbf u=\langle 3,4,0\rangle$ onto $\mathbf v=\langle 1,0,0\rangle$, which is $\dfrac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}$.
solution: $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=3$ and $\|\mathbf v\|=1$, so the projection is $3$.
hints: Divide the dot product by the length of $\mathbf v$.

prompt: Let $\mathbf u=\langle x,2,1\rangle$ and $\mathbf v=\langle 3,y,-1\rangle$. Write $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v$ as an expression in $x$ and $y$.
solution: $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=3x+2y-1$. Pair the components in order and add.
hints: Pair components in order.

prompt: Which pairs of vectors are orthogonal? Select all that apply.
solution: The dot products are $2-2+0=0$ and $0+0+0=0$. The other two give $1$ and $3$.
hints: Compute each dot product and check for zero.

prompt: Which vector is normal to the plane $2x-y+3z=6$?

why: used the constant $6$ as a coefficient

solution: For $ax+by+cz=d$ the normal is $\langle a,b,c\rangle$. The constant $d$ does not enter.
hints: Read the coefficients of $x$, $y$, and $z$ directly.

prompt: A line passes through $P(1,0,2)$ and $Q(4,3,-1)$. Which vector is parallel to the line?

why: added the points instead of subtracting
used a point, not a direction

solution: A direction is $Q-P=\langle 3,3,-3\rangle$.
hints: Subtract the coordinates of the two points.

prompt: The plane $2x+3y+4z=12$ meets the $z$-axis at $z=c$. Find $c$.
solution: Set $x=y=0$. Then $4z=12$, so $c=3$.
hints: Set the other two variables to zero.

prompt: The plane $2x-y+4z=d$ passes through $(1,2,3)$. Find $d$.
hints: Substitute the point into the left side.

prompt: Find the distance from the origin to the plane $2x+2y+z=9$.
solution: Distance $=\dfrac{|9|}{\sqrt{4+4+1}}=\dfrac{9}{3}=3$.
hints: Use $\dfrac{|d|}{\|\langle a,b,c\rangle\|}$.

prompt: The line $\mathbf r(t)=\langle 1+2t,\,-t,\,3+t\rangle$ meets the plane $x+y+z=10$ at $t=t_0$. Find $t_0$.
hints: Substitute the line's coordinates into the plane equation.

prompt: A line through $(1,2,3)$ has direction $\langle 4,-1,5\rangle$. Write its $y$-coordinate at parameter $t$ as an expression in $t$.
hints: Add the direction times $t$ to the point.

prompt: Find the $y$-intercept of the plane $3x+4y+6z=24$.
solution: Set $x=z=0$. Then $4y=24$, so $y=6$.
hints: Set $x$ and $z$ to zero.

prompt: Which of these points lie on the plane $2x-3y+z=4$? Select all that apply.
solution: $(1,0,2)$ gives $4$ and $(2,2,6)$ gives $4$. The others give $0$.
hints: Substitute each point into the left side.

prompt: What does $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(a,b)$ measure?

options: The rate of change of $f$ as $x$ varies, with $y$ held at $b$
The rate of change of $f$ as $y$ varies, with $x$ held at $a$
The rate of change of $f$ along the line $y=x$
why: swapped which variable is held fixed
a directional derivative, not a partial

solution: A partial derivative differentiates in one variable and treats the others as constants.
hints: The variable you differentiate is the only one that moves.

prompt: If $f_{xy}$ and $f_{yx}$ are continuous near a point, which equation holds there?

why: confuses mixed partials with equal second partials
mixed partials are equal, not opposite
adds first partials instead of differentiating

solution: Clairaut's theorem: continuous mixed partials agree.
hints: Order of differentiation does not matter here.

prompt: If $f(x,y)=x^3$, what is $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$?
solution: $f$ does not depend on $y$, so $f_y=0$.
hints: Treat $x$ as a constant when differentiating with respect to $y$.

prompt: Let $f(x,y)=x^2y^3$. Find $f_x(2,1)$.
hints: Differentiate in $x$ with $y$ constant.

prompt: Let $f(x,y)=xe^{xy}$. Find $f_y(1,0)$.
solution: $f_y=x\cdot xe^{xy}=x^2e^{xy}$. At $(1,0)$ this is $1$.
hints: Differentiate $e^{xy}$ with the chain rule.

prompt: Let $f(x,y)=\sin(xy)+x^2$. Write $f_x$ as an expression in $x$ and $y$.
solution: $f_x=y\cos(xy)+2x$. The chain rule gives the factor $y$.
hints: Differentiate $\sin(xy)$ with respect to $x$ first.

prompt: Let $z=\dfrac{x}{y}$. Find $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ at $(4,2)$.
hints: Write $x/y$ as $xy^{-1}$.

prompt: Let $f(x,y)=x^3y^2$. Find $f_{xy}(1,2)$.
hints: Differentiate in $y$ after $x$.

prompt: Which functions satisfy $f_x=0$ everywhere? Select all that apply.
solution: $f=y^2$ and $f=\sin y$ do not depend on $x$. The others change with $x$.
hints: Ask whether $x$ appears in the formula.

prompt: If $z=f(x(t),y(t))$, which formula gives $\dfrac{dz}{dt}$?

why: used $x$ and $y$ instead of their derivatives
multiplied the terms instead of adding

solution: Each intermediate variable contributes a partial times a derivative. The contributions add.
hints: Sum one term for each intermediate variable.

prompt: If $w=g(u)$ and $u=h(x,y)$, which equals $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x}$?

why: left $g$ instead of $g'$ on the outer function
added the factors instead of multiplying

solution: The outer derivative is evaluated at $u$, then multiplied by the inner partial.
hints: Multiply the outer derivative by the inner derivative.

prompt: Let $z=f(x,y)$ with $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t)$. Suppose $f_x(1,2)=3$, $x'(0)=2$, $y'(0)=0$, $x(0)=1$, and $y(0)=2$. Find $\dfrac{dz}{dt}$ at $t=0$.
solution: $\dfrac{dz}{dt}=f_x\,x'+f_y\,y'=3\cdot2+f_y\cdot0=6$.
hints: The $y$ term vanishes because $y'(0)=0$.

prompt: Let $z=x^2+xy$, $x=t^2$, and $y=t$. Find $\dfrac{dz}{dt}$ at $t=1$.
hints: Evaluate partials and derivatives at $t=1$ before combining.

prompt: Let $w=xyz$ with $x=t$, $y=t^2$, and $z=t^3$. Find $\dfrac{dw}{dt}$ at $t=1$.
solution: $w=t^6$, so $dw/dt=6t^5$, which is $6$ at $t=1$.
hints: Write $w$ in terms of $t$ first.

prompt: Let $z=e^{x-y}$, $x=2s$, and $y=s$. Write $\dfrac{dz}{ds}$ as an expression in $s$.
hints: Write $x-y$ in terms of $s$ before differentiating.

prompt: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at $(3,4)$ on the circle $x^2+y^2=25$.
solution: Implicitly, $2x+2y\,y'=0$, so $y'=-x/y=-3/4$.
hints: Treat $y$ as a function of $x$ and use the chain rule.

prompt: Let $z=x^2+y^2$ with $x=r$ and $y=2r$. Find $\dfrac{dz}{dr}$ at $r=1$.
hints: Evaluate $y$ at $r=1$, not at $r=0$.

prompt: Let $w=u^3$ with $u=s^2t$. Write $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s}$ as an expression in $s$ and $t$.
solution: $w=s^6t^3$, so $\partial w/\partial s=6s^5t^3$. The chain rule gives $3u^2\cdot2st$, the same thing.
hints: Use $\partial w/\partial s=3u^2\,\partial u/\partial s$.

prompt:
In which direction does $
abla f$ point, where $
abla f
eq\mathbf 0$?

options: Tangent to the level curve through the point
why: the gradient is perpendicular to level curves, not tangent
zero rate of change, which is the level-curve direction

solution: The gradient gives the direction of fastest increase. Its length is that rate.
hints: Compare with the one-variable slope.

prompt: Which expression gives the directional derivative of $f$ in the direction of a unit vector $\mathbf u$?

why: cross product gives a vector, not a rate
adds vectors and gives no rate

solution: $D_{\mathbf u}f=\nabla f\cdot\mathbf u$ when $\mathbf u$ is a unit vector.
hints: Dot the gradient with the direction.

prompt: At a point where $\nabla f=\langle 6,8\rangle$, what is the maximum value of the directional derivative?
solution: The maximum is $\|\nabla f\|=\sqrt{36+64}=10$.
hints: The maximum is the length of the gradient.

prompt: Let $f=x^2y$. Find $D_{\mathbf u}f(1,2)$ where $\mathbf u=\langle 3,4\rangle/5$.
solution: $\nabla f=\langle 2xy,x^2\rangle=\langle4,1\rangle$ at $(1,2)$. Then $\nabla f\cdot\mathbf u=\frac{12+4}{5}=\frac{16}{5}$.
hints: Compute the gradient at the point first.

prompt: Let $f=x^2+3xy$. Find the sum of the components of $\nabla f$ at $(1,2)$.
solution: $\nabla f=\langle 2x+3y,\,3x\rangle$. At $(1,2)$ it is $\langle 8,3\rangle$, and $8+3=11$.
hints: Differentiate in each variable separately.

prompt: Let $f=x^2+y^2$. Find $\|\nabla f\|$ at $(3,4)$.
solution: $\nabla f=\langle 2x,2y\rangle=\langle 6,8\rangle$, whose length is $10$.
hints: Find the gradient at the point, then take its length.

prompt: Let $f=xy$. Write $D_{\mathbf u}f$ for $\mathbf u=\langle 1,1\rangle/\sqrt2$ as an expression in $x$ and $y$.
solution: $\nabla f=\langle y,x\rangle$. Dot with $\langle1,1\rangle/\sqrt2$ to get $(x+y)/\sqrt2$.
hints: Dot the gradient with the unit vector.

prompt: Let $f=x^2y+y^3$. Find the directional derivative of $f$ at $(2,1)$ in the direction of $\mathbf v=\langle 0,-2\rangle$.
solution: $\nabla f=\langle 2xy,\,x^2+3y^2\rangle=\langle4,7\rangle$ at $(2,1)$. The unit vector is $\langle0,-1\rangle$, so $D_{\mathbf v}f=-7$.
hints: Normalize $\mathbf v$ before the dot product.

prompt: Which statements about $\nabla f$ are true when $f$ is differentiable? Select all that apply.

options: It points in the direction of greatest increase of $f$
Its length equals the smallest rate of change of $f$
It is perpendicular to level curves of $f$
It is the zero vector at every critical point of $f$

solution: The gradient points uphill, is normal to level curves, and vanishes at critical points. Its length is the largest rate, not the smallest.
hints: Test each claim with $f=x^2+y^2$ at a point.

prompt: At a critical point, $D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2>0$ and $f_{xx}>0$. What is the point?

why: the test is inconclusive only when $D=0$

solution: A positive $D$ with $f_{xx}>0$ means $f$ curves up in every direction.
hints: Check the sign of $f_{xx}$ after $D$.

prompt: At a critical point with $D<0$, the point is a:
solution: When $D<0$, $f$ rises in one direction and falls in another.
hints: Compare with $x^2-y^2$.

prompt: At a critical point, $f_{xx}=4$, $f_{yy}=9$, and $f_{xy}=6$. Find $D$.
solution: $D=36-36=0$, so the second derivative test is inconclusive.
hints: Compute $f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2$.

prompt: Find the value $f$ takes at the critical point of $f=x^2+y^2-4x+6y$.
hints: Set both partials to zero.

prompt: Let $f=x^3-3x+y^2$. How many of its critical points are saddle points?
solution: Critical points are $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$. There $D=12x$, which is $12$ at $(1,0)$ (minimum) and $-12$ at $(-1,0)$ (saddle).
hints: Compute $D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2$ at each critical point.

prompt: Find the maximum of $f=xy$ on the triangle $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$, $x+y\le 6$.
solution: The only interior critical point is the origin, where $f=0$. On $x+y=6$, $f=x(6-x)$, which is largest at $x=3$, giving $9$.
hints: Check the edges, since the interior has no useful critical point.

prompt: Let $f=x^2y+y^2$. Write $D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2$ as an expression in $x$ and $y$.
hints: Compute the three second partials first.

prompt: Find the critical value of $f=x^2-2xy+3y^2-2x$.
hints: Solve the two linear equations.

prompt: For $f=x^2+4y^2$, which statements are true? Select all that apply.
solution: Both partials vanish at the origin. Since $f\ge0$ with $f=0$ only there, the origin is a local and global minimum.
hints: Compare $f$ with its value at the origin.

prompt: To extremize $f$ subject to $g(x,y)=c$, which system holds at the optimum, where $\nabla g\neq\mathbf 0$?

why: $\lambda$ multiplies the gradient, not the value of $g$
$\nabla f$ need not vanish at a constrained extremum

solution: At a constrained extremum, $\nabla f$ is parallel to $\nabla g$, and the constraint holds.
hints: The gradients line up at the optimum.

prompt: In a Lagrange problem, what does the multiplier $\lambda$ measure?

options: Rate of change of the optimal value of $f$ as $c$ changes
The value of $f$ at the optimum
why: that is $f$ itself, not its sensitivity
$\nabla g$ is a vector, and $\lambda$ is a scalar
$\lambda$ is zero only when the constraint is inactive

solution: $\lambda$ is the sensitivity of the optimal value to the constraint level.
hints: Change $c$ slightly and see what happens to the optimum.

prompt: Maximize $xy$ subject to $x+y=10$. At the optimum, what is $x$?
solution: $\nabla f=\langle y,x\rangle=\lambda\langle1,1\rangle$ gives $x=y$. With $x+y=10$, $x=5$.
hints: Set the gradient components equal.

prompt: Minimize $x^2+y^2$ subject to $x+y=4$. Find the minimum value.
solution: $2x=\lambda$ and $2y=\lambda$, so $x=y=2$. The minimum is $4+4=8$.
hints: Set $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$ and use the constraint.

prompt: Maximize $xy$ subject to $x+2y=8$. Find the maximum value.
solution: $\nabla f=\langle y,x\rangle=\lambda\langle1,2\rangle$, so $x=2y$. Then $4y=8$, giving $y=2$, $x=4$, and $xy=8$.
hints: Match the gradient of $f$ to the gradient of $g$.

prompt: Maximize $x+y$ on the circle $x^2+y^2=8$. Find the maximum value.
solution: The gradient condition gives $x=y$. Then $2x^2=8$ and $x=2$, so $x+y=4$.
hints: Use $x=y$ from the gradient condition.

prompt: Minimize $x^2+y^2$ subject to $x+y=4$. Using $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$, find the multiplier $\lambda$ at the optimum.
solution: From $2x=\lambda$ and $x=2$, we get $\lambda=4$.
hints: Use the first component of $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$.

prompt: Minimize $x^2+y^2$ subject to $x+y=c$. Write the optimal $x$ as an expression in $c$.
solution: $x=y$ and $2x=c$. So $x=c/2$.
hints: Use the constraint to solve for $x$ after finding $x=y$.

prompt: Which statements are necessary at a constrained extremum of $f$ on $g=0$, when $\nabla g\neq\mathbf 0$? Select all that apply.
solution:
The constraint must hold, and $
abla f$ must be parallel to $
abla g$. $
abla f$ need not vanish.
hints: Test whether each condition is required at every constrained extremum.

prompt: For a continuous $f$ on a rectangle $R$, Fubini's theorem says $\iint_R f\,dA$:

options: Can be computed as an iterated integral in either order
Always equals the product of two single integrals
Equals the average of $f$ at the corners times the area
why: one order alone does not give the double integral
corner values do not give the integral

solution: For continuous integrands on rectangles, the order of integration can be chosen freely.
hints: The order can change, but the answer cannot.

prompt: Which iterated integral gives the area of $\{a\le x\le b,\ g_1(x)\le y\le g_2(x)\}$?

why: inner variable does not match the $y$-bounds
integrand $x$ is not the area element

solution: The inner bounds are in $y$, so the inner integral is $dy$. Its integrand is $1$.
hints: Match the inner variable to the bounds.

prompt: Find the area of the rectangle $[0,3]\times[0,2]$ using a double integral.
solution: $\int_0^3\int_0^2 dy\,dx=3\cdot2=6$.
hints: Integrate $1$ over the rectangle.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\int_0^2 xy\,dy\,dx$.
solution: $\int_0^2 xy\,dy=2x$. Then $\int_0^1 2x\,dx=1$.
hints: Integrate in $y$ first, treating $x$ as a constant.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\int_x^1 dy\,dx$.
solution: The inner integral is $1-x$. Then $\int_0^1(1-x)\,dx=\frac12$, the area of the triangle.
hints: Sketch the region first.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\int_0^x y\,dy\,dx$.
solution: $\int_0^x y\,dy=\frac{x^2}{2}$. Then $\int_0^1 \frac{x^2}{2}\,dx=\frac16$.
hints: Integrate in $y$ first, then use the bounds for $x$.

prompt: Evaluate the inner integral $\displaystyle\int_0^x (x+y)\,dy$ as an expression in $x$.
hints: Treat $x$ as a constant in the inner integral.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\iint_T 2\,dA$, where $T$ is the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(3,0)$, and $(0,3)$.
solution: The area of $T$ is $\frac92$. Multiply by the constant $2$ to get $9$.
hints: Compute the area, then multiply by the integrand.

prompt: Which expressions give the area of the region between $y=x$ and $y=x^2$ for $0\le x\le 1$? Select all that apply.
solution: On $[0,1]$ the top curve is $y=x$ and the bottom is $y=x^2$. The area is $\int_0^1(x-x^2)\,dx=\frac16$.
hints: The upper bound must be the larger function.

prompt: What is the Jacobian $\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)}$ for $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$?

why: squared $r$ instead of taking the determinant

solution: The determinant is $r\cos^2\theta+r\sin^2\theta=r$.
hints: Compute the $2\times2$ determinant of partials.

prompt: What is the volume element $dV$ in spherical coordinates $(\rho,\phi,\theta)$?

why: wrong power of $\rho$ in the Jacobian

solution: The spherical Jacobian is $\rho^2\sin\phi$.
hints: Include the $\sin\phi$ factor from the spherical shell.

prompt: In cylindrical coordinates, $dV=F(r)\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$. Write $F(r)$ as an expression in $r$.
solution: The cylindrical Jacobian is $r$, the same as the polar Jacobian.
hints: It equals the polar Jacobian.

prompt: Write $x^2+y^2$ in polar coordinates as an expression in $r$.
solution: $x^2+y^2=r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)=r^2$.
hints: Use $\cos^2+\sin^2=1$.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\iint_D x\,dA$, where $D=\{x^2+y^2\le1,\ x\ge0\}$.
solution: In polar form, $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_0^1 (r\cos\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta=2\cdot\frac13=\frac23$.
hints: Convert $x$ and $dA$ to polar before integrating.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^1\int_0^2 z\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$. Give a decimal.
solution: The integral separates into $\frac{\pi}{2}\cdot\frac12\cdot2=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
hints: Integrate each variable separately.

prompt: Write $x^2+y^2+z^2$ in cylindrical coordinates as an expression in $r$ and $z$.
solution: $x^2+y^2=r^2$, so the sum is $r^2+z^2$.
hints: Replace $x^2+y^2$ by $r^2$.

prompt: Use spherical coordinates to find the volume of the unit ball. Give the answer as a decimal.
solution: $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi}\int_0^1\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=\frac{4\pi}{3}$.
hints: Multiply the three separate integrals.

prompt: Which integrals equal the area of the unit disk? Select all that apply.
solution: The first and third both give $\pi$. The second omits $r$, and the last integrates over the square $[-1,1]^2$, with area $4$.
hints: Check the Jacobian and the region.

prompt: For $z=f(x,y)\ge0$ over a region $D$, which integral gives the volume under the surface?

why: gives the area of $D$, not the volume
a single line integral, not a volume

solution: Each small column has base $dA$ and height $f(x,y)$.
hints: Volume is base area times height.

prompt: For a box $[a,b]\times[c,d]\times[e,f]$ and continuous $g$, how can $\iiint g\,dV$ be computed?

options: As an iterated integral in any order of $dx$, $dy$, $dz$
Always as a product of three single integrals
By averaging $g$ at the eight corners
why: any order works for a box
product form needs a separable integrand
corner values do not give the integral

solution: Fubini's theorem allows any order of iterated integration on a box.
hints: Order can change for continuous integrands on boxes.

prompt: Find the volume of the box $[0,2]\times[0,3]\times[0,4]$.
solution: $2\cdot3\cdot4=24$.
hints: Multiply the three side lengths.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\int_0^1\int_0^1 (x+y+z)\,dx\,dy\,dz$.
solution: Each term integrates to $\frac12$ over the unit cube, so the total is $\frac32$.
hints: Integrate one term at a time.

prompt: Find the volume of the tetrahedron $x,y,z\ge0$ with $x+y+z\le1$.
solution: $\int_0^1\int_0^{1-x}\int_0^{1-x-y}dz\,dy\,dx=\frac16$.
hints: Use $z$ from $0$ to $1-x-y$ first.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\int_0^1\int_0^1 xyz\,dV$.
solution: Each variable contributes $\int_0^1 t\,dt=\frac12$, so the product is $\frac18$.
hints: Each variable separates.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{y} z\,dz$ as an expression in $y$.
solution: $\int_0^y z\,dz=\frac{y^2}{2}$.
hints: Integrate $z$ with respect to $z$.

prompt: Let $E=\{0\le x\le1,\ 0\le y\le x,\ 0\le z\le2\}$. Find $\iiint_E 1\,dV$.
solution: The base triangle has area $\frac12$ and the height is $2$, so the volume is $1$.
hints: Find the base area first, then multiply by the height.

prompt: Which integrals give the volume of the tetrahedron with vertices $(0,0,0)$, $(1,0,0)$, $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,1)$? Select all that apply.
solution: The region is $x,y,z\ge0$ with $x+y+z\le1$. The third integral covers it in another order. The cube and the last integral describe other solids.
hints: Each valid integral has upper limits that sum to $1$.

prompt: If $\mathbf F=\nabla\varphi$ on a curve $C$ from $A$ to $B$, what is $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$?
solution: The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives the difference of potential at the endpoints.
hints: Compare with $\int_a^b f'=f(b)-f(a)$.

prompt: On a simply connected planar domain, which condition makes $\mathbf F=\langle P,Q\rangle$ conservative?

why: equal components do not imply conservative

solution: The curl test $Q_x=P_y$ characterizes conservative fields on such domains.
hints: Check the mixed partials.

prompt: What is $\displaystyle\oint_C\nabla\varphi\cdot d\mathbf r$ for a closed curve $C$ and smooth $\varphi$?
solution: The endpoints coincide, so $\varphi(B)-\varphi(A)=0$.
hints: A closed loop starts and ends at the same point.

prompt: Let $\mathbf F=\langle y,x\rangle$. Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$ along the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$.
solution: $\mathbf F=\nabla(xy)$, so the integral is $\varphi(1,1)-\varphi(0,0)=1$.
hints: Find a potential first.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_C 2x\,dx+y\,dy$, where $C$ is $y=x^2$ from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$.
solution: Substitute $y=x^2$ and $dy=2x\,dx$: $\int_0^1(2x+2x^3)\,dx=1+\frac12=\frac32$.
hints: Parametrize by $x$.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_C x\,dy$ along the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(2,4)$.
solution: Use $x=2t$, $y=4t$ for $0\le t\le1$. Then $\int_0^1 8t\,dt=4$.
hints: Parametrize the segment.

prompt: Give a potential $\varphi(x,y)$ with $\varphi(0,0)=0$ for $\mathbf F=\langle 2xy,\ x^2+3y^2\rangle$.
solution: $\varphi_x=2xy$ and $\varphi_y=x^2+3y^2$ give $\varphi=x^2y+y^3$.
hints: Integrate $P$ in $x$, then fix the rest from $Q$.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_C x^2\,dx$ along the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,2)$.
solution: Parametrize by $x=t$, $y=2t$. Then $\int_0^1 t^2\,dt=\frac13$.
hints: Parametrize the segment.

prompt: Which vector fields on $\mathbb R^2$ are conservative? Select all that apply.
solution: $\langle y,x\rangle$ and $\langle 2x,2y\rangle$ pass the test $Q_x=P_y$. The other two fail it.
hints: Compare $Q_x$ with $P_y$.

prompt: What does Green's theorem state for a positively oriented simple closed curve $C$ bounding $D$?

why: adds mixed partials instead of subtracting
divergence belongs to the flux form

solution: The line integral equals the double integral of $Q_x-P_y$ over the enclosed region.
hints: Check the derivative on $Q$ first.

prompt: Which hypothesis is required for Green's theorem on a region $D$?

options: $C$ is positively oriented, simple, closed, piecewise smooth, and $P$, $Q$ have continuous partials on $D$
why: any simple closed curve needs no extra condition
conservative fields give zero, not a general rule
any region with a boundary works

solution: Green's theorem covers any such region, not only circles and rectangles.
hints: Check which hypothesis the theorem needs, not which shape it prefers.

prompt: Suppose $Q_x-P_y=4$ on a region $D$ of area $3$. What is $\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy$ for the boundary $C$?
solution: By Green's theorem, the integral equals $\iint_D 4\,dA=4\cdot3=12$.
hints: Multiply the integrand by the area.

prompt: Let $C$ be the boundary of $[0,1]^2$, counterclockwise. Evaluate $\oint_C -y\,dx+x\,dy$.
solution: $Q_x-P_y=1-(-1)=2$. The area is $1$, so the integral is $2$.
hints: Compute $Q_x-P_y$ first.

prompt: Let $C$ be the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, counterclockwise. Evaluate $\oint_C x^2\,dy$.
solution: $Q_x=2x$, so the double integral is $\int_0^1\int_0^{1-x}2x\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1 2x(1-x)\,dx=\frac13$.
hints: Integrate $Q_x$ over the triangle.

prompt: Use Green's theorem on the boundary of the unit disk, counterclockwise, to find the area of the disk from $\oint_C x\,dy$. Give a decimal.
solution: $Q_x-P_y=1$, so the integral equals the area $\pi$.
hints: Find $Q_x-P_y$ first.

prompt: For $P=x^2y$ and $Q=xy^2$, write $Q_x-P_y$ as an expression in $x$ and $y$.
solution: $Q_x=y^2$ and $P_y=x^2$.
hints: Differentiate $Q$ in $x$ and $P$ in $y$.

prompt: Let $C$ be the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(0,2)$, counterclockwise. Evaluate $\oint_C y\,dx$.
solution: $Q_x-P_y=0-1=-1$, and the area is $2$. The integral is $-2$.
hints: Compute $Q_x-P_y$ first.

prompt: Which statements about Green's theorem are true? Select all that apply.

options: It converts a line integral over $C$ into a double integral over the region inside $C$
It applies to curves that cross themselves

solution: Positive orientation is needed. The theorem turns the boundary integral into a double integral. It applies to simple curves, not self-crossing ones, and does not require $P_y=Q_x$.
hints: Check each claim against the hypotheses.

prompt: For $\mathbf F=\langle P,Q,R\rangle$, what is $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F$?

why: pairs the components with the wrong variables
sums the components, not their derivatives

solution: Divergence sums each component's derivative in its own variable.
hints: Each component is paired with its own variable.

prompt: What is the curl of a conservative field $\mathbf F=\nabla\varphi$?

why: curl of a gradient is zero, not a constant
curl of a gradient is zero, not $\mathbf F$

solution: The curl of any gradient is the zero vector.
hints: Curl of a gradient vanishes.

prompt: What is $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf F)$ for a smooth field $\mathbf F$?
solution: The divergence of a curl is always zero for smooth fields.
hints: Expand both operators and compare mixed partials.

prompt: Find $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F$ at $(1,2,3)$ for $\mathbf F=\langle x^2,y^2,z^2\rangle$.
solution: $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=2x+2y+2z$, which is $12$ at $(1,2,3)$.
hints: Differentiate each component in its own variable.

prompt: For $\mathbf F=\langle -y,x,0\rangle$, find the $z$-component of $\nabla\times\mathbf F$.
solution: The $z$-component is $Q_x-P_y=1-(-1)=2$.
hints: Use $Q_x-P_y$.

prompt: Write $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F$ as an expression in $x,y,z$ for $\mathbf F=\langle xy,\ yz,\ zx\rangle$.
solution: $P_x=y$, $Q_y=z$, $R_z=x$. The sum is $x+y+z$.
hints: Differentiate each component in its own variable.

prompt: Find the flux of $\mathbf F=\langle x,0,0\rangle$ outward through the face $x=1$ of the cube $[0,1]^3$.
solution: On $x=1$, $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n=1$. The face has area $1$, so the flux is $1$.
hints: Dot $\mathbf F$ with the outward normal.

prompt: Find the $z$-component of $\nabla\times\mathbf F$ at $(1,2)$ for $\mathbf F=\langle x^2y,\ xy^2,\ 0\rangle$.
hints: Compute $Q_x-P_y$ and then substitute.

prompt: Which statements are true for smooth fields and functions? Select all that apply.
solution: Both identities hold for smooth functions. The Laplacian of $f$ is generally nonzero. The curl of a field in space is a vector.
hints: Test each identity on a simple example.

prompt: What does Stokes' theorem relate?

options: Circulation of $\mathbf F$ around $\partial S$ to the flux of $\nabla\times\mathbf F$ through $S$
Flux through a closed surface to a triple integral of $\nabla\times\mathbf F$
Two line integrals over the same curve
why: mixes up the divergence theorem with the curl
divergence, not curl, belongs in this surface integral

solution: Stokes' theorem equates circulation around a boundary with the flux of the curl through the surface.
hints: Match the curve integral to the surface integral.

prompt: What does the divergence theorem state for a closed surface $S$ bounding a solid $E$?

options: Outward flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ equals $\displaystyle\iiint_E \nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV$
Outward flux equals $\displaystyle\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$
why: curl is a vector and does not integrate to flux
Stokes' form, which needs a boundary curve
a line integral, which needs a curve

solution: Outward flux equals the triple integral of the divergence over the enclosed solid.
hints: Divergence goes with solids, curl goes with surfaces.

prompt: A solid $E$ has volume $2$, and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=5$ throughout. What is the outward flux through its boundary?
solution: The divergence theorem gives $\iiint_E 5\,dV=5\cdot2=10$.
hints: Multiply the divergence by the volume.

prompt: Find the outward flux of $\mathbf F=\langle x^2,y^2,z^2\rangle$ through the boundary of $[0,1]^3$.
solution: $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=2x+2y+2z$. Its integral over the cube is $1+1+1=3$.
hints: Integrate the divergence over the cube.

prompt: Let $C$ be the boundary of $[0,1]^2$ in the plane $z=0$, counterclockwise. For $\mathbf F=\langle y,0,0\rangle$, find $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$.
solution: The curl's $z$-component is $0-1=-1$. The square has area $1$, so Stokes gives $-1$.
hints: Use the $z$-component of the curl.

prompt: Find the outward flux of $\mathbf F=\langle 0,0,z^3\rangle$ through the boundary of $[0,1]^3$.
solution: $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=3z^2$. Integrating over the cube gives $\int_0^1 3z^2\,dz=1$.
hints: Only $z$ matters in the divergence.

prompt: Write $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F$ as an expression in $x$ and $z$ for $\mathbf F=\langle x^2z,\ y,\ 0\rangle$.
solution: $P_x=2xz$, $Q_y=1$, and $R_z=0$. The sum is $2xz+1$.
hints: Differentiate each component in its own variable.

prompt: Let $C$ be the boundary of $[0,1]^2$ in the plane $z=0$, counterclockwise. For $\mathbf F=\langle -y,x,0\rangle$, find $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$.
solution: The $z$-component of the curl is $2$. Over a unit square, Stokes gives $2$.
hints: Compute the $z$-component of the curl first.

prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options: Stokes' theorem needs the surface orientation to match the boundary orientation
The divergence theorem needs $S$ to be a closed surface
Stokes' theorem on a closed surface gives a nonzero result in general
The divergence theorem computes a circulation around a curve

solution: Stokes needs a boundary with matching orientation. A closed surface has no boundary, so its Stokes integral is zero. The divergence theorem gives flux, not circulation.
hints: Check each claim against the hypotheses.

prompt: Vectors $\mathbf u,\mathbf v\in\mathbb R^3$ satisfy $|\mathbf u|=2$, $|\mathbf v|=3$ and $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=3$. What is the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf u+\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf u-\mathbf v$?

why: forgot the factor $2$ in $(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)\times(\mathbf u-\mathbf v)=-2\,\mathbf u\times\mathbf v$
used $|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|^2=|\mathbf u|^2|\mathbf v|^2-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v$ without squaring the dot product
used $2\,\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v$ as the area

rubric.text: Cross product expanded: $(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)\times(\mathbf u-\mathbf v)=-2\,\mathbf u\times\mathbf v$
$|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|^2=|\mathbf u|^2|\mathbf v|^2-(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)^2=27$ via $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$

solution:
Expand using antisymmetry: $(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)\times(\mathbf u-\mathbf v)=-\mathbf u\times\mathbf v+\mathbf v\times\mathbf u=-2\,\mathbf u\times\mathbf v$ (vec-ops).
Lagrange identity: $|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|^2=|\mathbf u|^2|\mathbf v|^2\sin^2\theta=|\mathbf u|^2|\mathbf v|^2-(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)^2=36-9=27$ (trig-id).
So $|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|=3\sqrt3$ and the area is $2\cdot3\sqrt3=6\sqrt3$.
hints: Expand the cross product first; the cross of $\mathbf u$ with itself vanishes.

prompt: Let $A=(1,0,0)$, $B=(0,2,0)$, $C=(0,0,3)$ and let $O$ be the origin. What is the distance from $O$ to the plane through $A$, $B$, $C$?

why: used height $=V/\text{area}$, missing the factor $3$ in $V=\frac13\,\text{area}\cdot h$
used triangle area $7$ instead of $\frac72$ (forgot the $\tfrac12$)

rubric.text: Tetrahedron volume $\tfrac16|\det|=1$ from the triple product

solution:
$\overrightarrow{AB}=(-1,2,0)$, $\overrightarrow{AC}=(-1,0,3)$; cross product $=(6,3,2)$, length $7$ (vec-ops).
Triangle area $=\tfrac72$.
Volume of $OABC$: $\tfrac16|\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot(\overrightarrow{OB}\times\overrightarrow{OC})|=\tfrac16\cdot6=1$ (geom-formulas).
$V=\tfrac13\,\text{area}\cdot h$ gives $h=3/(7/2)=6/7$.
Check: plane $6x+3y+2z=6$, distance $6/\sqrt{49}$.
hints: Compute the volume of the tetrahedron $OABC$ two ways: triple product and base times height.

prompt: Line $L_1$ passes through $(1,0,0)$ with direction $(1,1,0)$. Line $L_2$ passes through $(0,0,2)$ with direction $(0,1,1)$. What is the shortest distance between $L_1$ and $L_2$?

why: divided by $|\mathbf n|^2$ instead of $|\mathbf n|$
did not normalise the common normal
used the distance between the base points
divided the base-point distance by $|\mathbf n|$ instead of projecting onto $\mathbf n$

solution:
Common normal: $\mathbf n=(1,1,0)\times(0,1,1)=(1,-1,1)$, $|\mathbf n|=\sqrt3$ (vec-ops).
Base-point difference: $(0,0,2)-(1,0,0)=(-1,0,2)$.
Distance $=|(-1,0,2)\cdot(1,-1,1)|/\sqrt3=1/\sqrt3$ (lines-planes: skew-line formula).
hints: The shortest segment is parallel to $\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2$.

prompt: The line $(x,y,z)=(1,0,3)+t(2,-1,1)$ meets the plane $2x-y+3z=19$ at $P$. Let $F$ be the point of that plane closest to the origin. What is $|PF|$?

why: gave $|OF|$, the distance from the origin to the plane
gave the parameter of $F$ along the normal

rubric.text: Distance to plane $|OF|=19/\sqrt{14}$ from the normal $(2,-1,3)$

solution:
Substitute the line into the plane (lines-planes): $2(1+2t)+t+3(3+t)=11+8t=19$, so $t=1$ and $P=(3,-1,4)$ (lin-eq).
$|OP|^2=9+1+16=26$.
$F$ lies along the normal $\mathbf n=(2,-1,3)$, $|OF|=19/|\mathbf n|=19/\sqrt{14}$ (vec-ops: projection).
$OF\perp FP$, so $|PF|^2=26-361/14=3/14$.
hints: $OF$ is perpendicular to the plane, so triangle $OFP$ has a right angle at $F$.

prompt: Let $f(x,y)=y\,e^{xy}$. What is $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}$ at the point $(1,2)$?

why: treated $e^{xy}$ as constant when differentiating in $y$, dropping the term $xy^2e^{xy}$
differentiated $e^{xy}$ with respect to $y$ as $y\,e^{xy}$ instead of $x\,e^{xy}$
evaluated the exponent $xy$ at $(1,1)$ instead of $(1,2)$

rubric.text: Mixed partials are equal, so either order is allowed

solution:
$f_x=y\cdot y\,e^{xy}=y^2e^{xy}$ (chain-rule: $\partial_x e^{xy}=y\,e^{xy}$).
$f_{xy}=\partial_y\big(y^2e^{xy}\big)=2y\,e^{xy}+y^2\cdot x\,e^{xy}$ (deriv-rules: product rule).
At $(1,2)$: $4e^2+4e^2=8e^2$.
The order does not matter since $f$ is $C^2$ (partials).
hints: Differentiate in $x$ first; then apply the product rule in $y$.

prompt: The equation $x^2+yz+z^3=3$ defines $z$ implicitly as a function of $x$ and $y$ near $(1,1,1)$. What is $\dfrac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x^2}$ at $(1,1)$?

why: sign error in the quotient-rule term: $-\frac12+\frac38$

solution:
Differentiate in $x$ (implicit): $2x+(y+3z^2)z_x=0$, so $z_x=-2x/(y+3z^2)$; at the point $z_x=-2/4=-\tfrac12$.
Differentiate $2x+(y+3z^2)z_x=0$ again in $x$ (partials): $2+6z\,z_x^2+(y+3z^2)z_{xx}=0$.
At $(1,1,1)$: $2+6\cdot\tfrac14+4z_{xx}=0$, so $z_{xx}=-\tfrac{7/2}{4}=-\tfrac78$.
hints: Differentiate the relation $2x+(y+3z^2)z_x=0$ again; do not solve for $z_x$ first.

prompt: Let $w=u\,e^{v}$ with $u=x^2-y$ and $v=xy$. What is $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x}$ at $(x,y)=(2,1)$?

rubric.text: Chain rule with two paths: $w_x=w_u u_x+w_v v_x$

hints: $x$ reaches $w$ through both $u$ and $v$.

prompt: The temperature at $(x,y,z)$ is $T=x^2+yz$. A particle moves along $\mathbf r(t)=(t,\,t^2,\,t^3)$. What is $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$ at $t=2$?

why: added the partials without multiplying by the velocity components
used the velocity at $t=1$, $(1,2,3)$, with the gradient at $t=2$

solution:
Gradient: $\nabla T=(2x,\,z,\,y)$; at $t=2$ the point is $(2,4,8)$, so $\nabla T=(4,8,4)$ (partials).
Velocity: $\mathbf r'(t)=(1,2t,3t^2)=(1,4,12)$.
$\frac{dT}{dt}=\nabla T\cdot\mathbf r'=4+32+48=84$ (mv-chain).
Check: $T(\mathbf r(t))=t^2+t^5$, derivative $2t+5t^4=4+80$ (related-rates).
hints: Dot the gradient with the velocity, both evaluated at $t=2$.

prompt: Let $f(x,y,z)=x^2y-yz^2$, $P=(1,2,1)$ and $Q=(3,3,0)$. What is the directional derivative of $f$ at $P$ in the direction from $P$ toward $Q$?

why: did not normalise the direction vector
divided by $|\mathbf v|^2=6$ instead of $|\mathbf v|$
computed $|\mathbf v|$ as $\sqrt{2^2+1^2}$, dropping the third component

solution:
$
abla f=(2xy,\,x^2-z^2,\,-2yz)$, so $
abla f(P)=(4,0,-4)$ (partials).
$\mathbf v=Q-P=(2,1,-1)$, $|\mathbf v|=\sqrt6$.
$D_{\mathbf u}f=
abla f\cdot\mathbf v/|\mathbf v|=(8+0+4)/\sqrt6=12/\sqrt6=2\sqrt6$ (gradient: unit direction).
hints: Normalise $Q-P$ before dotting with the gradient.

prompt: The tangent plane to the surface $z=x^2+y^2$ at some point is parallel to the plane $2x+4y-z=7$. What is the $z$-intercept of that tangent plane?

why: sign error: wrote the plane as $z=2x+4y+5$
dropped the height $z_0=5$ of the point from the tangent plane equation

rubric.text: Normal to the level surface $g=z-x^2-y^2$: $\nabla g=(-2x,-2y,1)$

solution:
Level surface $g=z-x^2-y^2=0$ has normal $\nabla g=(-2x,-2y,1)$ (gradient).
Parallel to $(2,4,-1)$ means $(-2x_0,-2y_0,1)=-(2,4,-1)$, so $x_0=1$, $y_0=2$, $z_0=5$.
Plane: $z-5=2(x-1)+4(y-2)$ (lines-planes), i.e. $z=2x+4y-5$.
Intercept at $x=y=0$: $-5$.
hints: Two planes are parallel exactly when their normals are parallel; normalise the $z$-coordinate.

prompt: The function $f(x,y)=x^3-3xy+y^3$ has exactly one local minimum. What is the value of $f$ there?

why: gave the value at the saddle point $(0,0)$

rubric.text: Second-derivative test: $D=36xy-9$ is negative at $(0,0)$, positive with $f_{xx}=6>0$ at $(1,1)$

solution:
$f_x=3x^2-3y=0$ and $f_y=3y^2-3x=0$ give $y=x^2$ and $x^4=x$ (partials, sys-eq).
Solutions: $x=0$ or $x=1$, so the critical points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.
$D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2=36xy-9$: $D(0,0)=-9<0$ is a saddle; $D(1,1)=27>0$ with $f_{xx}=6>0$ is a local minimum (mv-extrema).
$f(1,1)=1-3+1=-1$.
hints: Solve $f_x=f_y=0$ by substituting $y=x^2$.

prompt: On the closed disk $x^2+y^2\le4$, let $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-2x$. What is the difference between the absolute maximum and the absolute minimum of $f$ on the disk?

why: took the minimum $0$ from the boundary and missed the interior critical point
added the minimum $-1$ to the maximum $8$
used $-2$ as the minimum, reading only $-2x$ at $x=1$
compared the interior value $-1$ with the boundary value $4$

solution:
Interior: $f_x=2x-2=0$, $f_y=2y=0$ give $(1,0)$, which lies in the disk, $f(1,0)=-1$ (mv-extrema).
Boundary $x^2+y^2=4$: $f=4-2x$ with $x\in[-2,2]$, so $f$ runs from $0$ (at $x=2$) to $8$ (at $x=-2$) (optimize: closed interval).
Candidates: $-1$, $0$, $8$. Maximum $8$, minimum $-1$, difference $9$.
hints: Check the interior critical points, then reduce $f$ on the boundary circle to one variable.

prompt: What is the maximum value of $f(x,y)=xy^2$ subject to $x^2+y^2=12$?

why: took $x=y=2$ (satisfies neither the constraint nor the multiplier equations)
used $x=2$ with $y^2=12$, the full constraint constant

solution:
$\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$: $y^2=2\lambda x$, $2xy=2\lambda y$ (lagrange).
If $y=0$ then $f=0$. Otherwise divide by $y$: $x=\lambda$, so $y^2=2x^2$.
Constraint: $x^2+2x^2=12$, so $x=\pm2$, $y^2=8$ (sys-eq).
$f=xy^2=\pm16$; the maximum is $16$ at $x=2$.
hints: Divide the second multiplier equation by $y$ after treating $y=0$ separately.

prompt: On the curve $x^2+xy+y^2=3$, what is the maximum value of $x^2+y^2$?

why: gave the minimum, from the direction $x=y$
gave the constant on the right-hand side
gave the maximum distance instead of its square
tested the lattice point $(2,-1)$ on the curve

solution:
Let $g=x^2+xy+y^2$. $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$: $2x=\lambda(2x+y)$, $2y=\lambda(x+2y)$ (lagrange).
Multiply the first by $y$, the second by $x$ and subtract: $2xy-2xy=\lambda(2xy+y^2-x^2-2xy)$, so $\lambda(y^2-x^2)=0$ (factor).
$\lambda=0$ forces $x=y=0$, off the curve, so $y=\pm x$.
$y=x$: $3x^2=3$, $x^2+y^2=2$. $y=-x$: $x^2=3$, $x^2+y^2=6$ (sys-eq). The maximum is $6$.
hints: Eliminate $\lambda$ by cross-multiplying the two gradient equations.

prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_x^1 e^{y^2}\,dy\,dx$.

why: dropped the lower-limit term $-\tfrac12$ from the antiderivative
sign error at the lower limit of $\tfrac12e^{y^2}$
replaced the integrand by $1$ (area of the triangle)

rubric.text: Recognise that $\int e^{y^2}dy$ has no elementary form, so swap the order
Region $0\le x\le y\le1$: integral becomes $\int_0^1 y\,e^{y^2}dy$

solution:
$e^{y^2}$ has no elementary antiderivative in $y$, so swap the order (double-int).
Region: $0\le x\le y$, $0\le y\le1$.
$\int_0^1\!\int_0^y e^{y^2}dx\,dy=\int_0^1 y\,e^{y^2}dy$.
$u=y^2$, $du=2y\,dy$ (u-sub): $\tfrac12\int_0^1e^u du=\tfrac{e-1}{2}$.
hints: Sketch the region and integrate in $x$ first.

prompt: Let $R$ be the region between $y=x^2$ and $y=\sqrt x$ for $0\le x\le1$. What is $\displaystyle\iint_R (x+y)\,dA$?
solution:
The curves meet at $x=0,1$ and $\sqrt x\ge x^2$ on $[0,1]$ (double-int: vertical slices).
Inner: $\int_{x^2}^{\sqrt x}(x+y)\,dy=x(\sqrt x-x^2)+\tfrac12(x-x^4)$.
Outer: $\int_0^1\big(x^{3/2}-x^3+\tfrac x2-\tfrac{x^4}2\big)dx=\tfrac25-\tfrac14+\tfrac14-\tfrac1{10}=\tfrac3{10}$ (area-volume: region between curves).
hints: Use vertical slices: $y$ from the lower curve to the upper one.

prompt: Let $D=\{(x,y): 1\le x^2+y^2\le4,\ y\ge0\}$. What is $\displaystyle\iint_D x^2\,dA$?

why: used the average $\tfrac14$ rather than $\tfrac12$ of $\cos^2\theta$

rubric.text: Angular integral $\int_0^\pi\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\tfrac\pi2$ via the half-angle identity

solution:
Polar (coord-change): $x^2\,dA=r^2\cos^2\theta\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta$, $1\le r\le2$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$.
Radial: $\int_1^2 r^3dr=\tfrac{16-1}{4}=\tfrac{15}4$.
Angular: $\int_0^\pi\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\int_0^\pi\tfrac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}d\theta=\tfrac\pi2$ (trig-int).
Product: $\tfrac{15}{4}\cdot\tfrac\pi2=\tfrac{15\pi}{8}$.
hints: Use polar coordinates; the integrand picks up $\cos^2\theta$ and the area element picks up $r$.

prompt: Let $B$ be the unit ball $x^2+y^2+z^2\le1$. What is $\displaystyle\iiint_B (x^2+y^2)\,dV$?

why: forgot the $\sin\varphi$ in the Jacobian, integrating $\sin^2\varphi$ instead of $\sin^3\varphi$

solution:
Spherical (coord-change): $x^2+y^2=\rho^2\sin^2\varphi$, $dV=\rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta$.
Integrand becomes $\rho^4\sin^3\varphi$, so the integral factors into $\int_0^1\rho^4d\rho\cdot\int_0^\pi\sin^3\varphi\,d\varphi\cdot\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta$.
$\int_0^\pi\sin^3\varphi\,d\varphi=\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^2)du=\tfrac43$ with $u=\cos\varphi$ (trig-id, trig-int).
Product: $\tfrac15\cdot\tfrac43\cdot2\pi=\tfrac{8\pi}{15}$.
hints: After the substitution the integral separates into three one-variable integrals.

prompt: Let $T$ be the tetrahedron $x,y,z\ge0$, $x+y+z\le1$. What is $\displaystyle\iiint_T x\,dV$?

why: forgot the $\tfrac12$ in the cross-section area $\tfrac{(1-x)^2}{2}$
used $\bar x=\tfrac34$ instead of $\tfrac14$ times volume $\tfrac16$

rubric.text: Slice at fixed $x$: triangle $y,z\ge0$, $y+z\le1-x$ with area $\tfrac{(1-x)^2}{2}$

solution:
Slice at fixed $x$ (triple-int): the $(y,z)$ cross-section is a right triangle with legs $1-x$, area $\tfrac{(1-x)^2}{2}$.
$\iiint x\,dV=\int_0^1x\cdot\tfrac{(1-x)^2}{2}\,dx=\tfrac12\int_0^1(x-2x^2+x^3)dx$.
$=\tfrac12\big(\tfrac12-\tfrac23+\tfrac14\big)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac1{12}=\tfrac1{24}$ (area-volume: slicing).
Check: $\bar x\cdot V=\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac16$.
hints: Integrate over a cross-section at fixed $x$ first; its area is a simple function of $x$.

prompt: What is the volume of the solid enclosed between the paraboloids $z=x^2+y^2$ and $z=8-x^2-y^2$?

why: used the plane $z=0$ as the bottom surface

solution:
Intersection: $r^2=8-r^2$, so $r=2$ (coord-change: cylindrical).
$V=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^2\!\!\int_{r^2}^{8-r^2}r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$ (triple-int).
$=2\pi\int_0^2(8-2r^2)r\,dr=2\pi\big[4r^2-\tfrac{r^4}{2}\big]_0^2=2\pi(16-8)=16\pi$ (area-volume).
hints: Use cylindrical coordinates; find where the surfaces meet first.

prompt: Let $\mathbf F=(2xy,\ x^2+z^2,\ 2yz)$ and let $C$ be the curve $\mathbf r(t)=(t,\,2t^2,\,3t^3)$, $0\le t\le1$. What is $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$?

why: used the potential $x^2y$ only, missing the $yz^2$ term
used the potential $yz^2$ only, missing the $x^2y$ term
added the coordinates of the endpoint $(1,2,3)$

rubric.text: Curl is zero (mixed partials agree), so $\mathbf F$ is conservative

solution:
Check conservativeness (partials): $\partial_y(2xy)=2x=\partial_x(x^2+z^2)$, $\partial_z(2xy)=0=\partial_x(2yz)$, $\partial_z(x^2+z^2)=2z=\partial_y(2yz)$.
Integrate: $f=x^2y+g(y,z)$, $f_y=x^2+z^2$ gives $g=yz^2+h(z)$, and $f_z=2yz$ gives $h'=0$. So $f=x^2y+yz^2$ (line-int: potential function).
The path runs from $(0,0,0)$ to $(1,2,3)$, so the integral is $f(1,2,3)-f(0,0,0)=2+18=20$ (gradient: fundamental theorem).
hints: Test whether $\mathbf F$ is a gradient before parametrising.

prompt: Let $\mathbf F=(y^2,\ x)$ and let $C$ be the parabola $y=x^2$ from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$. What is $\displaystyle\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$?

rubric.text: $\mathbf F$ is not conservative ($\partial_x x=1\neq 2y=\partial_y y^2$), so the path matters

solution:
Curl check: $Q_x-P_y=1-2y\neq0$, so the value depends on the path (line-int).
Parametrise: $x=t$, $y=t^2$, $dx=dt$, $dy=2t\,dt$, $0\le t\le1$.
$\int P\,dx+Q\,dy=\int_0^1\big(t^4+t\cdot2t\big)dt=\int_0^1(t^4+2t^2)dt$ (antideriv).
$=\tfrac15+\tfrac23=\tfrac{13}{15}$.
hints: Substitute $y=x^2$ and $dy=2x\,dx$ into $y^2\,dx+x\,dy$.

prompt: Let $C$ be the circle $x^2+y^2=4$, traversed counterclockwise. What is $\displaystyle\oint_C\big(-y^3\,dx+x^3\,dy\big)$?

why: forgot the Jacobian $r$ in the polar integral

solution:
$P=-y^3$, $Q=x^3$: $Q_x-P_y=3x^2+3y^2$ (green).
Counterclockwise boundary of the disk: $\oint=\iint_D3(x^2+y^2)\,dA$.
Polar (coord-change): $\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^23r^2\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta=2\pi\cdot3\cdot4=24\pi$.
hints: Convert the circulation to an area integral and then to polar coordinates.

prompt: The astroid $x=\cos^3t$, $y=\sin^3t$, $0\le t\le2\pi$, bounds a region. What is its area?

why: gave the area of the circumscribed unit disk

solution:
Green (green): $A=\tfrac12\oint(x\,dy-y\,dx)$, counterclockwise.
$dx=-3\cos^2t\sin t\,dt$, $dy=3\sin^2t\cos t\,dt$ (param-polar).
$x\,dy-y\,dx=3\cos^4t\sin^2t+3\sin^4t\cos^2t=3\sin^2t\cos^2t\,dt$.
$\sin^2t\cos^2t=\tfrac14\sin^22t$ with average $\tfrac18$, so $\int_0^{2\pi}=\tfrac\pi4$ (trig-int).
$A=\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot\tfrac\pi4=\tfrac{3\pi}8$.
hints: Use $A=\tfrac12\oint x\,dy-y\,dx$ and simplify with $\cos^2+\sin^2=1$.

prompt: The field $\mathbf F=(a\,xy+z^3,\ x^2+2yz,\ b\,xz^2+y^2)$ is conservative for suitable constants $a,b$. What is $\operatorname{div}\mathbf F$ at $(1,2,1)$?

why: found $b=1$ from the wrong curl component

solution:
Curl-free: $\partial_yF_1=\partial_xF_2$ gives $ax=2x$, so $a=2$ (div-curl).
$\partial_zF_1=\partial_xF_3$ gives $3z^2=bz^2$, so $b=3$. The third condition $\partial_zF_2=2y=\partial_yF_3$ holds automatically.
$\operatorname{div}\mathbf F=\partial_x(2xy+z^3)+\partial_y(x^2+2yz)+\partial_z(3xz^2+y^2)=2y+2z+6xz$ (partials).
At $(1,2,1)$: $4+2+6=12$.
hints: Use the curl conditions to pin down $a$ and $b$ first.

prompt: Let $S$ be the part of the paraboloid $z=4-x^2-y^2$ with $z\ge0$, oriented upward. What is the flux $\displaystyle\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S$ of $\mathbf F=(x,\,y,\,1)$ through $S$?

why: dropped the $+1$ from the $z$-component of $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n$
used $(-2x,-2y,1)$ as the upward normal, so the $x,y$ parts flipped sign

rubric.text: $\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=(2x^2+2y^2+1)\,dA$ over the disk $r\le2$

solution:
For $z=g(x,y)$ with upward orientation, $d\mathbf S=(-g_x,-g_y,1)\,dA=(2x,2y,1)\,dA$ (div-curl: surface integral).
$\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=(2x^2+2y^2+1)\,dA$ over the projection $x^2+y^2\le4$ (double-int).
Polar (coord-change): $\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^2(2r^2+1)\,r\,dr\,d\theta=2\pi\big[\tfrac{r^4}{2}+\tfrac{r^2}{2}\big]_0^2=2\pi(8+2)=20\pi$.
hints: Write the surface as a graph and use $d\mathbf S=(-g_x,-g_y,1)\,dA$.

prompt: Let $S$ be the unit sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ with outward orientation. What is $\displaystyle\iint_S(x^3,\,y^3,\,z^3)\cdot d\mathbf S$?

why: forgot the Jacobian $\rho^2$ in the volume integral
used $\rho^3$ in place of $\rho^2$ in the Jacobian

rubric.text: Divergence theorem applies to the closed surface

solution:
The surface is closed, so Gauss applies (stokes-gauss): $\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=\iiint_B\operatorname{div}\mathbf F\,dV$.
$\operatorname{div}\mathbf F=3(x^2+y^2+z^2)=3\rho^2$ (div-curl).
Spherical (coord-change): $\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^\pi\!\!\int_0^1 3\rho^2\cdot\rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta=3\cdot\tfrac15\cdot2\cdot2\pi=\tfrac{12\pi}{5}$.
hints: Convert the flux through the closed surface into a volume integral of the divergence.

prompt: Let $C$ be the curve where the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ meets the plane $z=x+y$, oriented counterclockwise when viewed from above. What is $\displaystyle\oint_C(z\,dx+x\,dy+y\,dz)$?

why: lost the sign: used $|\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n|$
used the unit normal but the flat disk area $\pi$ instead of the tilted area $\sqrt3\,\pi$
assumed the field is conservative because $\mathbf F$ is linear

rubric.text: Stokes: $\oint\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\iint\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S$ with $\mathbf F=(z,x,y)$ and $\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F=(1,1,1)$
Upward normal element on $z=x+y$: $d\mathbf S=(-1,-1,1)\,dA$, so the integrand is $-1$
Projection is the unit disk of area $\pi$, giving $-\pi$

solution:
$\mathbf F=(z,x,y)$ gives $\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F=(\partial_yF_3-\partial_zF_2,\ \partial_zF_1-\partial_xF_3,\ \partial_xF_2-\partial_yF_1)=(1,1,1)$ (div-curl).
Use the planar surface $z=x+y$ over the unit disk. Counterclockwise from above means upward normal: $d\mathbf S=(-z_x,-z_y,1)\,dA=(-1,-1,1)\,dA$ (stokes-gauss).
$\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=-1\,dA$, so the integral is $-1\cdot\text{area}(\text{unit disk})=-\pi$ (double-int).
Direct check: with $\mathbf r=(\cos t,\sin t,\cos t+\sin t)$ the integrand is $\cos^2t-2\sin^2t$, which integrates to $\pi-2\pi=-\pi$.
hints: Apply Stokes with the planar surface $z=x+y$ and its upward normal.

prompt: If $A$ is $2\times 3$ and $B$ is $3\times 4$, what is the size of $AB$?

why: used the inner size $3$ as the answer

solution: $AB$ takes the row count of $A$ and the column count of $B$, so $2\times 4$. The inner $3$ is summed out.
hints: Rows of $A$ meet columns of $B$.

prompt: Give the trace of $\begin{pmatrix}2&7\\-3&5\end{pmatrix}$.
solution: The trace adds the diagonal entries: $2+5=7$.
hints: Trace is the sum of the diagonal.

prompt: Which equals $(AB)^T$?
solution: The transpose of a product reverses the order: $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$.
hints: Transpose reverses the order of factors.

prompt: Find the $(2,1)$ entry of $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&5\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$.
solution: Row $2$ of the first matrix $(3,4)$ dotted with column $1$ of the second $(0,1)$ gives $4$.
hints: Entry $(i,j)$ is row $i$ dotted with column $j$.

prompt: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, find the $(1,2)$ entry of $A^2$.
solution: $A^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so the $(1,2)$ entry is $4$.
hints: Compute the product $A\cdot A$ row by column.

prompt: For a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with diagonal entries $a$ and $d$, simplify $\operatorname{tr}(3A)$.
solution: The trace is linear, so $\operatorname{tr}(3A)=3\operatorname{tr}A=3(a+d)$.
hints: Scalars pull out of the trace.

prompt: Find $\operatorname{tr}(A^2)$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$.
solution: $A^2=\begin{pmatrix}7&10\\15&22\end{pmatrix}$, and $7+22=29$.
hints: Square the matrix first, then take the trace.

prompt: If $A$ is $2\times 2$ with $\operatorname{tr}A=t$ and $\det A=d$, write $\operatorname{tr}(A^2)$ in terms of $t$ and $d$.
solution: For $2\times2$ matrices, $\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=(\operatorname{tr}A)^2-2\det A$.
hints: Use the eigenvalues: their squares add to $(\text{sum})^2-2(\text{product})$.

prompt: Which statements hold for every pair of $2\times 2$ matrices $A,B$?
solution: Trace is cyclic and linear, and transpose is additive. Matrix products do not commute, and transpose reverses products.
hints: Test a noncommuting pair.

prompt: Which row operation can change the solution set of a linear system?

options: Add a multiple of one row to another
why: thought reordering equations changes the solutions
thought row addition changes the solutions
thought a negative multiplier changes the solutions

solution: Multiplying by $0$ erases an equation. The other three are reversible.
hints: Ask whether the operation can be undone.

prompt: A row echelon form of a $3\times 4$ matrix has pivots only in columns $1$ and $3$. What is its rank?
solution: The rank equals the number of pivots, which is $2$.
hints: Count the pivots.

prompt: Which row operation takes $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ to echelon form with a zero row?
solution: Row $2$ minus $2\times$ row $1$ gives $(0,0)$, a zero row.
hints: Make the entry below the pivot zero.

prompt: Solve $x+2y=5$ and $3x+4y=6$ by row reduction. Find $y$.
solution: Subtract $3\times$ the first equation from the second: $-2y=-9$, so $y=\frac92$.
hints: Eliminate $x$ first.

prompt: A system has the echelon form $x+y+z=6$, $y+2z=5$, $z=2$. Find $x$.
solution: Back substitution: $z=2$, then $y=1$, then $x=6-1-2=3$.
hints: Substitute from the bottom row up.

prompt: Find the rank of $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&7\\3&6&10\end{pmatrix}$.
solution: Row $2$ minus $2\times$ row $1$ gives $(0,0,1)$. Row $3$ minus $3\times$ row $1$ gives $(0,0,1)$ too. Two pivots remain.
hints: Look for a repeated row after elimination.

prompt: Which augmented matrices are in reduced row echelon form?
solution: Reduced form needs leading $1$s moving right, zeros above and below each pivot. The second matrix has pivots out of order, the third has a nonzero above a pivot, and the fifth has a leading $2$.
hints: Check the entries above each pivot.

prompt: Row-reduce $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&k\end{pmatrix}$ by $R_2\to R_2-3R_1$. Give the new $(2,2)$ entry.
solution: The $(2,2)$ entry becomes $k-3\cdot2=k-6$.
hints: Multiply the pivot row by the multiplier before subtracting.

prompt: A system has augmented matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&|&3\\2&4&|&6\end{pmatrix}$. How many free variables does it have?
solution: Two unknowns and one pivot give $2-1=1$ free variable.
hints: Free variables are the unknowns without pivots.

prompt: What is $\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$?

why: swapped $c$ and $d$ in the bottom row

solution: The determinant is the product of the main diagonal minus the product of the off diagonal.
hints: Subtract the off-diagonal product.

prompt: A matrix has two equal rows. What is its determinant?
solution: Equal rows make the determinant zero, since a row operation can create a zero row.
hints: Subtract one row from the other.

prompt: Which is true of $\det(AB)$ for $n\times n$ matrices $A,B$?
solution: The determinant is multiplicative: $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$.
hints: Determinants multiply across products.

prompt: Find $\det\begin{pmatrix}3&-1\\4&2\end{pmatrix}$.
hints: Use $ad-bc$.

prompt: Find $\det\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\5&3&0\\1&7&4\end{pmatrix}$.
solution: The matrix is lower triangular, so the determinant is the product of the diagonal: $2\cdot3\cdot4=24$.
hints: Triangular matrices have easy determinants.

prompt: For a $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ with $\det A=5$, find $\det(2A)$.
solution: Scaling a $3\times3$ matrix by $2$ multiplies each of its three rows by $2$. So $\det(2A)=2^3\cdot5=40$.
hints: Each row contributes a factor of the scalar.

prompt: For $3\times 3$ matrices with $\det A=3$ and $\det B=-2$, find $\det(AB^T)$.
solution: Transposes keep the determinant and products multiply: $3\cdot(-2)=-6$.
hints: Use multiplicativity and $\det B^T=\det B$.

prompt: Find the determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\1&t\end{pmatrix}$ as a function of $t$.
solution: $\det=t\cdot t-1\cdot1=t^2-1$.
hints: Multiply the diagonal, subtract the off-diagonal product.

prompt: Which row operations leave $\det A$ unchanged?

options: Add a multiple of one row to another

solution: Adding a multiple of a row keeps the determinant. Multiplying by $1$ keeps it too. A swap flips the sign, and scaling by $2$ doubles it.
hints: Track each operation's effect on the determinant.

prompt: When $ad-bc\neq0$, what is $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}^{-1}$?
solution: Swap $a$ and $d$, negate $b$ and $c$, and divide by the determinant.
hints: Swap the diagonal and negate the off-diagonal.

prompt: If $\det A=x\neq0$, what is $\det(A^{-1})$?
solution: $\det(A^{-1})=\frac{1}{\det A}$, since $\det A\cdot\det A^{-1}=\det I=1$.
hints: Use multiplicativity with $AA^{-1}=I$.

prompt: If $A$ is invertible and $AB=AC$, what follows?
solution: Multiply on the left by $A^{-1}$: $B=A^{-1}AB=A^{-1}AC=C$.
hints: Multiply both sides by the inverse on the left.

prompt: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, find the $(2,2)$ entry of $A^{-1}$.
solution: $\det A=1$, so $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$. The $(2,2)$ entry is $2$.
hints: Use $\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$.

prompt: If $\det A=\frac25$, find $\det(A^{-1})$.
hints: Take the reciprocal.

prompt: Solve $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf b=(3,2)$. Find $x_1$.
solution: $\mathbf x=A^{-1}\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
hints: Multiply $\mathbf b$ by the inverse.

prompt: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with $t>\tfrac12$, write $\det(A^{-1})$ as a function of $t$.
hints: Compute $\det A$ first, then take its reciprocal.

prompt: Find the $(1,2)$ entry of $\begin{pmatrix}3&5\\1&2\end{pmatrix}^{-1}$.
solution: $\det=6-5=1$, so the inverse is $\begin{pmatrix}2&-5\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}$. Its $(1,2)$ entry is $-5$.
hints: Negate the off-diagonal entries and swap the diagonal.

prompt: Which of these matrices are invertible?
solution: Invertible means nonzero determinant. The first, third and fifth have determinant $0$. The second has $-2$ and the fourth has $6$.
hints: Compute each determinant.

prompt: Which is NOT required for a subset $W$ of $\mathbb R^n$ to be a subspace?

why: assumed a subspace must contain unit vectors

solution: A subspace needs $\mathbf 0$ and closure under addition and scalar multiplication. Unit vectors are not required.
hints: Check the three closure conditions only.

prompt: How many vectors does the zero subspace of $\mathbb R^3$ contain?
solution: The zero subspace is $\{\mathbf 0\}$, which has one element.
hints: It holds only the zero vector.

prompt: Which set is a subspace of $\mathbb R^2$?
solution: The line $y=2x$ passes through the origin and is closed under both operations.
hints: Does the set contain $\mathbf 0$?

prompt: The solutions of $x-y+z=0$ in $\mathbb R^3$ form a subspace. What is its dimension?
solution: One equation in three unknowns leaves two free variables, so the dimension is $2$.
hints: Dimension is the number of free variables.

prompt: Which of these sets are subspaces of $\mathbb R^3$?
solution: Planes through the origin defined by linear equations are subspaces. $x=1$ misses $\mathbf 0$. The set $xyz=0$ is a union of planes, not closed under addition.
hints: Check $\mathbf 0$ and closure for each equation.

prompt: Let $W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2),(2,4)\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$. What is $\dim W$?
solution: $(2,4)=2(1,2)$, so the two vectors span a line. The dimension is $1$.
hints: Check whether one vector is a multiple of the other.

prompt: Find $\dim W$ for $W=\{(x,y,z): x+y+z=0,\ z=0\}$.
solution: Two independent equations in three unknowns leave $3-2=1$ free variable.
hints: Count the independent equations.

prompt: Which is a subspace of $P_2$, the polynomials of degree at most $2$?
solution: Vanishing at $0$ is a linear condition, so the set is closed under addition and scalars.
hints: A linear condition on $p$ gives a subspace.

prompt: $U$ and $W$ are subspaces of $\mathbb R^4$ with $\dim U=3$, $\dim W=3$, and $U+W=\mathbb R^4$. Find $\dim(U\cap W)$.
solution: Dimension formula: $\dim(U+W)=\dim U+\dim W-\dim(U\cap W)$. So $4=6-\dim(U\cap W)$, giving $2$.
hints: Use the sum-of-dimensions formula.

prompt: How many vectors are in a basis of $\mathbb R^4$?
solution: A basis of $\mathbb R^n$ has $n$ vectors.
hints: A basis size equals the dimension.

prompt: What does it mean for vectors to be linearly independent?

options: No vector is a multiple of another
why: checks pairs only, not every combination

solution: Independence means $c_1\mathbf v_1+\cdots+c_k\mathbf v_k=\mathbf 0$ forces all $c_i=0$.
hints: Check all combinations, not pairs.

prompt: A set of $4$ vectors in $\mathbb R^3$ is always:

why: confused the count with a basis of $\mathbb R^4$

solution: More than $\dim=3$ vectors cannot be independent.
hints: Compare the count with the dimension.

prompt: Find $\dim\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,3),(2,4,6),(0,1,1)\}$.
solution: $(2,4,6)=2(1,2,3)$, so only two directions remain. They are independent, so the dimension is $2$.
hints: Remove vectors that are multiples of others.

prompt: Find $\dim\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1),(1,0,1)\}$.
solution: The determinant of the $3\times3$ matrix with these columns is $2\neq0$, so the vectors are independent. The dimension is $3$.
hints: Test with a determinant or row reduction.

prompt: Which of these sets is a basis of $\mathbb R^2$?
solution: A basis of $\mathbb R^2$ has two independent vectors. $(2,2)$ is a multiple of $(1,1)$, $\{(1,0)\}$ is too short, and three vectors are too many. The determinant of the third pair is $-2$.
hints: Two vectors, nonzero determinant.

prompt: The vectors $(1,k,0)$, $(0,1,1)$, $(1,0,2)$ in $\mathbb R^3$ are dependent. Find $k$.
solution: The determinant is $1(2-0)-k(0-1)=2+k$. Setting it to zero gives $k=-2$.
hints: Set the determinant of the matrix to zero.

prompt: Which is a basis of the plane $x+y+z=0$ in $\mathbb R^3$?

why: used $(1,1,1)$, which is not on the plane
used three vectors in a 2-dimensional space

solution: Both vectors satisfy $x+y+z=0$ and they are not parallel, so they form a basis.
hints: Check each vector against the plane equation.

prompt: Find the rank of the matrix with columns $(1,2,0)$, $(2,4,1)$, $(3,6,1)$.
solution: The third column is $3(1,2,0)+(0,0,1)$ and the second is $2(1,2,0)+(0,0,1)$. The span has dimension $2$.
hints: Look for columns that are combinations of others.

prompt: A linear map $\mathbb R^5\to\mathbb R^3$ has rank $2$. What is its nullity?
solution: Rank plus nullity equals the dimension of the domain: $2+\text{nullity}=5$, so nullity $3$.
hints: Nullity is the domain dimension minus rank.

prompt: For a linear map $T:V\to W$ with $V$ finite-dimensional, which holds?

why: used the codomain instead of the domain

solution: Rank-nullity: the image and kernel together account for all of $V$.
hints: Sum the kernel and image dimensions.

prompt: An $m\times n$ matrix has rank $r$. What is its nullity?
solution: The null space lives in $\mathbb R^n$, so nullity is $n-r$.
hints: The domain is $\mathbb R^n$.

prompt: A $4\times7$ matrix has rank $3$. What is the dimension of its null space?
solution: Nullity is columns minus rank: $7-3=4$.
hints: Columns, not rows, set the domain.

prompt: A $5\times6$ matrix has a $2$-dimensional null space. Find its rank.
hints: Rank plus nullity equals the number of columns.

prompt: Let $T(x,y,z)=(x+y,\,y+z,\,x+z)$ on $\mathbb R^3$. Find $\dim\ker T$.
solution: The matrix has determinant $2\neq0$, so $T$ is one-to-one and the kernel is $\{\mathbf 0\}$.
hints: Check whether the matrix is invertible.

prompt: A linear map $T:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^2$ is onto. Find $\dim\ker T$.
solution: Onto means rank $2$. So nullity is $4-2=2$.
hints: Onto fixes the rank at the codomain dimension.

prompt: Which statements hold for every linear map $T:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^5$?
solution: Rank is at most the domain dimension, and nullity is nonnegative. Rank plus nullity is $3$. The map can be one-to-one, and it cannot be onto since the rank is at most $3<5$.
hints: Use rank-nullity with domain dimension $3$.

prompt: Let $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ have $\dim\ker T=k$. Write $\operatorname{rank}T$ in terms of $n$ and $k$.
solution: Rank-nullity gives $\operatorname{rank}T=n-k$.
hints: Subtract the nullity from the domain dimension.

prompt: Which property defines a linear map $T$?
solution: Additivity and homogeneity together define linearity.
hints: Check both properties.

prompt: Let $T(x,y)=(2x,3y)$. What is the second coordinate of $T(1,1)$?
hints: Apply the formula to $(1,1)$.

prompt: For $T(x,y)=(x+y,\,x-y)$, what is the first column of its standard matrix?

why: read the second row instead of the column

solution: The first column is $T(e_1)=T(1,0)=(1,1)$.
hints: Columns are images of basis vectors.

prompt: $T(x,y)=(x+2y,\,3x)$. Find the $(2,1)$ entry of its matrix.
solution: The matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&0\end{pmatrix}$. Its $(2,1)$ entry is $3$.
hints: Read off the coefficients of each output coordinate.

prompt: A map $T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Write the first coordinate of $T(0,1)$ in terms of $t$.
solution: $T(0,1)$ is the second column $(t,1)$.
hints: The second column is the image of $e_2$.

prompt: A linear map has $T(1,0)=(2,5)$ and $T(0,1)=(-1,3)$. Find the second coordinate of $T(3,2)$.
hints: Use linearity on the basis vectors.

prompt: Which map is linear?
solution: Each coordinate of $(x-y,2x)$ is a linear form in $x,y$.
hints: Look for products of variables and constant shifts.

prompt: A linear map $\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ has matrix with rows $(1,0,2)$, $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,3)$. Find its determinant.
solution: The matrix is upper triangular, so the determinant is $1\cdot1\cdot3=3$.
hints: Triangular matrices give the determinant as a diagonal product.

prompt: For $T(x,y)=(x+y,\,0)$ on $\mathbb R^2$, which statements are true?
solution: The kernel is the line $x+y=0$, the image is the horizontal axis, and rank is $1$. The map is not one-to-one and not onto.
hints: Find the kernel and image directly.

prompt: If $A$ and $B$ represent the same map in two bases, with $B=P^{-1}AP$, what is the relation?

why: congruence $P^TAP$ matches similarity only when $P$ is orthogonal

solution: Similarity means $B=P^{-1}AP$ for an invertible $P$.
hints: Similar matrices are conjugates.

prompt: Similar matrices have the same trace. If $\operatorname{tr}A=7$ and $B=P^{-1}AP$, what is $\operatorname{tr}B$?
solution: Trace is invariant under similarity.
hints: Trace is preserved under change of basis.

prompt: If $P$ has the new basis vectors as columns, which product turns new coordinates into standard coordinates?

why: gives new coordinates from standard ones
wrong order: dimensions do not match

solution: Columns of $P$ are the basis vectors, so $P$ times the coordinates gives the vector.
hints: Columns of $P$ are the new basis.

prompt: Basis $B=\{(1,1),(1,-1)\}$. Find the first $B$-coordinate $c_1$ of $\mathbf v=(3,1)$.
hints: Solve a 2-by-2 system.

prompt: With the same basis $B=\{(1,1),(1,-1)\}$, find the second $B$-coordinate of $\mathbf v=(5,-1)$.
hints: Use the same system with new right sides.

prompt: Let $P=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&5\end{pmatrix}$. Find the $(1,2)$ entry of $P^{-1}AP$ as a function of $t$.
solution: $P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $P^{-1}AP=\begin{pmatrix}2&-3t\\0&5\end{pmatrix}$.
hints: Multiply in order: $P^{-1}$, then $A$, then $P$.

prompt: Which matrices are similar to $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$?
solution: Similar matrices share eigenvalues. $\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$ is a reordering. The upper triangular matrix has distinct eigenvalues $1,2$, so it is diagonalizable to the same form. The other two have different eigenvalues.
hints: Compare eigenvalues.

prompt: $P^{-1}AP$ is similar to $A$. If $\det A=6$ and $\det P=4$, find $\det(P^{-1}AP)$.
solution: $\det(P^{-1}AP)=\det(P)^{-1}\det(A)\det(P)=\det A=6$.
hints: Determinant is invariant under similarity.

prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $P^{-1}=P$. Which matrix is $P^{-1}AP$?

why: left $A$ unchanged: no change of basis
multiplied by $P$ on one side only

solution: $PA$ swaps the rows, then multiplying by $P$ on the right swaps the columns. The result is $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$.
hints: Swap rows, then swap columns.

prompt: For a $2\times2$ matrix $A$, which is the characteristic polynomial?

why: sign error on the trace term
sign error on the determinant term

solution: For $2\times2$ matrices, $\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)\lambda+\det A$.
hints: The coefficients are the trace and determinant.

prompt: A $2\times2$ matrix has trace $-4$. What is the sum of its eigenvalues?
